clue.text: Radical features of Whitman's leaves?

parts.note: Walt Whitman's poems are Leaves of Grass; the parts of a plant that are radical, in the old sense of belonging to the root, are its roots, and the phrase also means the ordinary members of a movement

explanation.surface: A literary critic asks what makes Whitman's poetry so radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radical' reads as politically extreme, but its Latin sense is 'of the root'; the features of grass at that level give the phrase for a movement's rank and file.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the ordinary people at the base of a political movement, the radical level in its root sense.

clue.text: The distress to which we come in reverse

definitions.text: The distress to which we come in reverse

parts.words: The distress to which we come in reverse
parts.note: a reverse is a setback, and the idiom for ending in disaster after one is to 'come to' this sorrow

explanation.surface: A gloomy line about the misery that follows a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In reverse' looks like a reversal signal, but here it means 'when suffering a reverse', a setback; the idiom is 'come to grief'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is deep sorrow or distress, and the idiom 'come to ...' means to meet with disaster.

clue.text: Fruit that at its best shows us many a wrinkle

definitions.text: Fruit that at its best shows us many a wrinkle

parts.words: Fruit that at its best shows us many a wrinkle
parts.note: an old English variety of eating fruit kept until shrivelled, when it was thought to be at its best

explanation.surface: A fruit that improves as it gets wrinkled, like a wise old face.
explanation.walkthrough: This is an old English apple, said to be ripe only around St John's Day and best eaten when its skin had withered; Shakespeare uses it for a wrinkled old man.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a variety of apple stored a long time, by which point its skin had shrivelled.

clue.text: Art is no work-a-day subject for them

definitions.text: Art is no work-a-day subject for them

parts.words: Art is no work-a-day subject for them
parts.note: amateur artists who paint only on their day off, the rest day of the week, not on working days

explanation.surface: A comment on people for whom art is anything but routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work-a-day' means ordinary, but read literally it is a working day; these hobby painters work on the one day that is not.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means amateur painters who take up the brush only at weekends, in their free time.

clue.text: Excel in trench warfare ?

parts.note: to surpass is to rise higher than something; in First World War trenches soldiers went 'over the top' of the parapet to attack

explanation.surface: A question about what it takes to shine in the trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: In the First World War, going 'over the top' meant climbing out of the trench to attack; the single word for that means to excel or rise above.
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass is to rise above another in height or merit, which is what excelling means.

clue.text: Fish if tinned can be fatal

definitions.meaning: the electric ray, a fish that numbs with a shock
tin fish is slang for the self-propelled naval missile, which can kill

explanation.surface: A warning that some canned fish can be deadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tinned' suggests canned food, but 'tin fish' is old naval slang for the weapon fired from a submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric ray is a fish that stuns its prey; a 'tin fish' is naval slang for the underwater missile fired from a submarine, which can sink a ship.

clue.text: No use trying to hit this nail on the head!

definitions.text: No use trying to hit this nail on the head!

parts.words: No use trying to hit this nail on the head!
parts.note: a thin small nail with little or no head, so it cannot be struck there

explanation.surface: A carpenter's warning that some nails are not worth aiming at.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'hit the nail on the head' means be exactly right; this slim flooring nail has almost no head to hit.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a thin nail with a tiny or no head, used for flooring and fine joinery.

clue.text: Marie Lloyd identified herself with one of these knockabout items

definitions.text: Marie Lloyd identified herself with one of these knockabout items

parts.words: Marie Lloyd identified herself with one of these knockabout items
parts.note: the music-hall song she sang was 'One of the ... That Cromwell Knocked About a Bit', remains of buildings Cromwell's troops battered

explanation.surface: A music-hall star compared herself to a battered prop.
explanation.walkthrough: Marie Lloyd was a British music-hall singer; her song 'One of the Ruins That Cromwell Knocked About a Bit' casts her as a crumbling building. 'Knockabout' suggests slapstick comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Remains of buildings wrecked long ago, such as castles Cromwell's army knocked down, are what the song names.

clue.text: With which we may expect a lead from the clergy ?

definitions.text: With which we may expect a lead from the clergy ?

parts.words: With which we may expect a lead from the clergy ?
parts.note: the white band a clergyman wears round the neck, which in a pet's case is what a lead clips to

explanation.surface: A question about where guidance from churchmen comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' suggests moral guidance, but a lead is also a leash, attached to the band round an animal's neck; clergy wear a band of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy wear a stiff white band round the neck known by the same name as a pet's neckband.

clue.text: Rummy object of a singer's devotion

definitions.text: Rummy object of a singer's devotion

parts.words: Rummy object of a singer's devotion
parts.note: an old drinking song praises a small brown pot of liquor, and 'rummy' is both 'odd' and 'full of rum'

explanation.surface: A singer is devoted to something rather odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rummy' reads as British slang for odd, but here it means holding rum; the drinking song 'Little Brown Jug' adores the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a popular drinking song is the vessel of liquor the singer adores.

clue.text: Encroach going back, for example, nip on to the motorway

indicators.note: going back says the string of pieces after it is read from its end to its start

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written here as MI

explanation.surface: Someone nips onto the motorway, reversing and encroaching on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going back' turns the whole run EG + NIP + MI round. The M1 is the London to Leeds motorway, with the figure 1 read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: To encroach is to intrude upon or trespass on something, a synonym.

clue.text: Support should one become ill in the enclosure

indicators.note: in puts the word for falling sick inside the word for an enclosure

parts.note: a ring is an enclosed arena, as in a boxing ring
to ail is to fall sick

explanation.surface: A fence offers support should someone feel unwell in the paddock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Should one' is linking padding; the enclosure is a boxing or circus ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence of bars, or a banister, gives support to lean on or hold.

clue.text: No cover charge, we hear, for Australian port

indicators.note: we hear says the phrase from the clue is a sound-alike of the place name

parts.note: a 'free mantle', a cloak given at no charge

explanation.surface: A traveller is told there is no cover charge at an Australian harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover charge' reads as a restaurant fee, but split it: a mantle is a cover, and free means no charge.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the port city near Perth in Western Australia, an example of the category.

clue.text: Poet has a cup and nothing more

parts.note: a tass is a Scots word for a small drinking cup
O, the round figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: A poet owns only a cup and nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: TASS is an old Scots word for a cup. 'Has a' and 'and ... more' link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso was the Italian Renaissance writer of verse who wrote Jerusalem Delivered, an example of the category.

clue.text: Fall out of love and languish

indicators.note: out of here means the word for a fall is built round the letter for love, made from it

parts.note: to drop is to fall
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Falling out of love leaves someone pining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall out of love' reads as a phrase, but split it: DROP is made out of, built round, O for love, the zero score in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop is to sag or flag, losing vigour, which is what languishing means.

clue.text: A show-place in Constable country

parts.note: Constable country is the Suffolk area John Constable painted; here a constable is a policeman, and the place is the setting of a TV police series

explanation.surface: A beauty spot in the region the painter Constable made famous.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable country is the Stour valley the painter John Constable painted; here it is policeman territory, the setting of the BBC TV series Dixon of Dock Green about a London police constable.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional London district was where the long-running BBC show about PC Dixon took place, a setting for a show.

clue.text: "Dance, and song, and sunburnt mirth " (Keats)

parts.note: the line in Ode to a Nightingale reads 'Dance, and ... song, and sunburnt mirth', with an adjective of the south of France missing before 'song'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Keats about dancing, singing and sunny merriment.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale has the line with this word before 'song'; it means from the southern French region famous for troubadours.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes the region of southern France known for its troubadour songs, which fills the gap in the quotation.

clue.text: He keeps your spirits down

parts.note: spirits are alcohol, and down means in the basement: the person in charge of an inn's or club's underground drink store

explanation.surface: A gloomy man who keeps dampening your mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps your spirits down' sounds like depressing you, but spirits are drink, kept below ground in a pub's cellar.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who looks after the beer and wine stored underground in a pub or hotel is this worker.

clue.text: They eat their own kind of food.

parts.words: They eat their own kind of food
parts.note: creatures, or people, who eat others of their own species, so their kind is their food

explanation.surface: Some people only eat their own sort of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Their own kind of food' reads as a preferred cuisine, but their own kind is the food: they eat their own species.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people or animals that eat the flesh of their own species.

clue.text: A self-disciplined tea-user might be this

indicators.note: might be this says the letters of the word before it could be rearranged into the description

explanation.surface: A tea drinker with strict self-control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might be this' invites rearranging TEA-USER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone strict and self-denying, avoiding comfort, is this.

clue.text: Can it weigh heavily on the conscience ?

definitions.text: Can it weigh heavily on the conscience ?

parts.words: Can it weigh heavily on the conscience ?
parts.note: the word is both a moral doubt that troubles the conscience and an old apothecaries' weight of twenty grains, a very light one

explanation.surface: A question about whether something could burden a guilty mind.
explanation.walkthrough: It is a qualm that can weigh on the conscience, but also an apothecaries' weight of 20 grains, too slight to weigh heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral qualm that weighs on the conscience is one sense; the other is a tiny old apothecaries' unit of weight.

clue.text: The linesman's the boss !

definitions.meaning: an instrument for drawing straight lines, so a thing that makes lines
a person in charge who governs

explanation.surface: In football, the linesman is in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' suggests a football official, but here it is something that draws lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight-edge for drawing lines is one sense; a monarch or leader in charge is the other.

clue.text: Walker, with pay for the players

definitions.text: Walker, with pay for the players

parts.words: Walker, with pay for the players
parts.note: a spirit that 'walks' haunting a place; theatre slang 'the ... walks' meant the actors were being paid

explanation.surface: A rambler who brings the actors' wages.
explanation.walkthrough: An old theatre saying, 'the ghost walks', meant payday had come, from Hamlet's ghost; a spirit also walks as it haunts.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit of the dead walks the earth, and in theatre slang its walking signalled the actors' payday.

clue.text: Tipsy, perhaps, having been bribed?

definitions.meaning: to oil someone's palm is to bribe them

explanation.surface: A tipsy official may have been paid off.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are slang: 'well-oiled' means drunk, and 'oiling the palm' means bribing.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for drunk is one sense; to 'grease the palm', give a bribe, is the other.

clue.text: Not the warders' dance, you crazy fellow

definitions.text: Not the warders' dance, you crazy fellow

parts.words: Not the warders' dance, you crazy fellow
parts.note: prison officers are called screws in British slang, so their dance would be the screws' ball; the word is really an eccentric person

explanation.surface: Someone insists this is not a party for prison guards.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a prison warder is a 'screw', so a dance for them would be a screws' ball; the word really means an eccentric.
explanation.definitionFit: An eccentric or crazy person is this, in American slang.

clue.text: Pays attention to the scene of contest

definitions.meaning: list is an archaic verb for listen
the palisaded ground where knights jousted

explanation.surface: A spectator pays attention to the arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'List' in the archaic sense means listen; knights fought in the lists, the jousting ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Old poetic 'list' means listen; the enclosed ground for medieval jousting is the other.

clue.text: Increase the likeness, in general

indicators.note: in here says the letters wanted are contained in the word general, rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter is asked to make the portrait bigger, generally speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In general' looks like 'on the whole', but the letters of GENERAL rearrange to the answer. 'Increase the likeness' means blow up a photo.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow up a photograph or portrait is to make it bigger.

clue.text: The cat's were the very thing!

definitions.text: The cat's were the very thing!

parts.words: The cat's were the very thing!
parts.note: the old slang phrase 'the cat's ...', like 'the cat's whiskers', meant something excellent; here it is the cat's nightwear

explanation.surface: A remark that the cat's outfit was just perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cat's pyjamas' is 1920s slang for something excellent, the very thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The garments worn for sleeping make the slang phrase meaning something excellent.

clue.text: Such a knot can be done, with difficulty

indicators.note: with difficulty suggests the word done is wrestled into a new order

explanation.surface: A tricky knot can be tied, with some effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With difficulty' rearranges DONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A knot or lump, as on a plant stem, is a node.

clue.text: They make clean break, get ten reds

indicators.note: break tells the solver to smash the following words apart and rebuild them

explanation.surface: Snooker: make a clean break, pot ten reds.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is snooker (a break of ten reds), but 'break' rearranges GET TEN REDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleaning agents such as washing powders are what make things clean.
